concepts.title: Ex Ante and Ex Post Measures
concepts.definition: Planned values of consumption, investment or output are ex ante quantities, while the values actually realised during the year are ex post; a producer intending to add 100 to stock who ends up adding 70 has ex ante investment of 100 but ex post investment of 70.
concepts.key_idea: Plans (ex ante) drive behaviour, outcomes (ex post) enter the accounts, and unplanned inventory change reconciles the two.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.1 opening and producer example, pages 54-55
question_patterns: differentiate planned investment from realised investment and explain the role of unplanned stock change
what do planned and actual values of a variable mean in macroeconomics
how do unintended changes in inventories reconcile plans with outcomes
a producer plans stock of 100 but sells 30 from stock, give planned and realised investment
which measure of a variable enters national income accounting
explain why planned output need not equal planned aggregate demand

solution_steps.action: Separate the plan from the outcome
solution_steps.explain: Ex ante is what agents intend before the period unfolds; ex post is what the accounts record after it closes.
When sales surprise the producer, the difference between planned and realised investment shows up as unintended inventory change.
Ask whether the figure was set in advance as a plan (ex ante) or measured after the fact (ex post).

concepts.title: Consumption Function
concepts.definition: Household consumption rises linearly with income: it has a floor of autonomous consumption that persists even at zero income, plus induced consumption equal to a fixed fraction of every extra rupee earned.
concepts.key_idea: The intercept is subsistence spending and the slope is the fraction of income consumed.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.1.1, equation 4.1 and Imagenia example, page 55
question_patterns: state the Keynesian relation between household spending and income with its autonomous floor and induced part
find household consumption when autonomous consumption the slope and income are given
what is consumed when income is zero and why
a country consumes 60 plus 0.75 times income, state the intercept and slope
how much does consumption rise when income increases by 100 with a given slope
graph the relation between spending and income marking its intercept and slope

solution_steps.action: Add the income-sensitive part to the floor
solution_steps.explain: Multiply income by the marginal propensity to consume for induced consumption, then add the autonomous part.

worked_examples.question: Using Consumption Function, compute the result for autonomous_consumption = 3, marginal_propensity_to_consume = 3, income = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add the income-sensitive part to the floor: consumption = autonomous_consumption + marginal_propensity_to_consume * income = 12.0 Final result: 12.0

worked_examples.question: Using Consumption Function, compute the result for autonomous_consumption = 4, marginal_propensity_to_consume = 4, income = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Add the income-sensitive part to the floor: consumption = autonomous_consumption + marginal_propensity_to_consume * income = 20.0 Final result: 20.0

concepts.title: Marginal Propensity to Consume and to Save
concepts.definition: The marginal propensity to consume is the fraction of any extra unit of income that gets spent, lying between 0 and 1; the remainder of the extra income is saved, so the marginal propensities to consume and save always sum to one.
concepts.key_idea: Of every additional rupee, one fraction is spent and the rest saved, and the two fractions exhaust the rupee.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.1.1, Some Definitions box, pages 55-56
question_patterns: compute the marginal propensity to consume from a change in income and consumption
find the marginal propensity to save when the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8
why must MPC and MPS add up to one
income rises from 500 to 600 and consumption from 450 to 525, find MPC and MPS
within what limits can the marginal propensity to consume vary
define the rate of change of consumption with respect to income

solution_steps.explain: Dividing the change in consumption by the change in income gives the marginal propensity to consume.
Subtracting the consume fraction from one leaves the share saved, the marginal propensity to save.

worked_examples.question: Using Marginal Propensity to Consume and to Save, compute the result for change_in_consumption = 3, change_in_income = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Ratio the two changes: marginal_propensity_to_consume = change_in_consumption / change_in_income = 1.0 Step 2: Take the unspent residue: marginal_propensity_to_save = 1 - marginal_propensity_to_consume = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.question: Using Marginal Propensity to Consume and to Save, compute the result for change_in_consumption = 4, change_in_income = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Ratio the two changes: marginal_propensity_to_consume = change_in_consumption / change_in_income = 1.0 Step 2: Take the unspent residue: marginal_propensity_to_save = 1 - marginal_propensity_to_consume = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

concepts.title: Average Propensity to Consume and to Save
concepts.definition: Average propensities look at totals rather than changes: the average propensity to consume is consumption per rupee of income and the average propensity to save is savings per rupee, and since savings equal unconsumed income the two averages also add to one.
concepts.key_idea: Averages split total income between consuming and saving; the split always sums to unity.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.1.1, Some Definitions box, page 56
question_patterns: calculate the average propensity to consume when consumption and income are given
find the average propensity to save from savings and income
how do average and marginal propensities differ
show that APC and APS must sum to one
a household earns 1000 and spends 850, give its APC and APS
define consumption and savings per unit of income

solution_steps.explain: The share of total income consumed is the average propensity to consume.

solution_steps.action: Find the saved share of income
solution_steps.explain: Savings equal income minus consumption; dividing savings by income gives the average propensity to save.
Savings over income is the average propensity to save, and it equals one minus the average propensity to consume.

worked_examples.question: Using Average Propensity to Consume and to Save, compute the result for consumption = 3, income = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Divide consumption by income: average_propensity_to_consume = consumption / income = 1.0 Step 2: Find the saved share of income: savings = income - consumption = 0.0 Step 3: Complete the split: average_propensity_to_save = savings / income = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.question: Using Average Propensity to Consume and to Save, compute the result for consumption = 4, income = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Divide consumption by income: average_propensity_to_consume = consumption / income = 1.0 Step 2: Find the saved share of income: savings = income - consumption = 0.0 Step 3: Complete the split: average_propensity_to_save = savings / income = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

concepts.title: Autonomous Investment
concepts.definition: In the short-run model, planned investment is treated as a given constant fixed by producers in advance - an addition to physical capital and inventories that does not vary with the current year's income.
concepts.key_idea: Investment goods add productive capacity for years, and here their planned amount is exogenous.
question_patterns: why is investment assumed autonomous in the simple model
what counts as investment in the national income sense
how does the interest rate influence the decision to invest
show planned investment as a horizontal line against income
distinguish investment goods from intermediate goods
state the investment behaviour assumed in the two-sector model

solution_steps.explain: Investment means adding to machines, buildings or inventories - assets that serve production over years, not inputs used up at once.
Planned investment is a fixed positive number chosen ahead of time, so it does not move with current income.
In reality credit availability and the interest rate govern investment, but the model holds them aside.

concepts.title: Aggregate Demand in the Two-Sector Model
concepts.definition: Without a government or foreign sector, planned demand for final goods is consumption plus investment, which expands to the sum of all autonomous spending plus the income-sensitive consumption term.
concepts.key_idea: Aggregate demand has a constant part (autonomous) and a part that grows with income (induced).
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.2, AD = C + I derivation, page 57
question_patterns: build aggregate demand for an economy with only households and firms
compute planned aggregate demand at a given income level
which parts of aggregate demand do not depend on income
add the consumption and investment functions to get the AD equation
why is the AD line parallel to the consumption function
measure ex ante aggregate demand when A and the slope and income are known

solution_steps.explain: Autonomous consumption plus autonomous investment form the constant term of demand.
Adding the slope times income gives total planned demand at that income.

worked_examples.question: Using Aggregate Demand in the Two-Sector Model, compute the result for autonomous_consumption = 3, autonomous_investment = 3, marginal_propensity_to_consume = 3, income = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Combine the autonomous outlays: autonomous_expenditure = autonomous_consumption + autonomous_investment = 6.0 Step 2: Attach the induced component: aggregate_demand = autonomous_expenditure + marginal_propensity_to_consume * income = 12.0 Final result: 12.0

worked_examples.question: Using Aggregate Demand in the Two-Sector Model, compute the result for autonomous_consumption = 4, autonomous_investment = 4, marginal_propensity_to_consume = 4, income = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Combine the autonomous outlays: autonomous_expenditure = autonomous_consumption + autonomous_investment = 8.0 Step 2: Attach the induced component: aggregate_demand = autonomous_expenditure + marginal_propensity_to_consume * income = 20.0 Final result: 20.0

concepts.title: Adding the Government: Taxes and Spending in Aggregate Demand
concepts.definition: With a government, taxes shave income down to disposable income and public spending adds to demand, so consumption depends on income after tax while government expenditure joins the autonomous term.
concepts.key_idea: Households spend out of income net of taxes, and G - cT behaves like extra autonomous demand.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.2, government modification paragraph, page 57
question_patterns: modify aggregate demand when the government taxes and spends
find disposable income after a lump-sum tax
compute planned demand with government expenditure and proportional consumption out of after-tax income
how do taxes reduce the induced part of aggregate demand
why does G minus cT act like autonomous expenditure
write the aggregate demand equation for a three-sector economy

solution_steps.explain: Disposable income is what households can spend after the tax deduction.

solution_steps.action: Assemble demand with the public sector
solution_steps.explain: Autonomous private spending plus government spending plus consumption out of disposable income gives aggregate demand.

worked_examples.question: Using Adding the Government: Taxes and Spending in Aggregate Demand, compute the result for income = 3, tax_revenue = 3, autonomous_expenditure = 3, government_spending = 2, marginal_propensity_to_consume = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Remove taxes from income: disposable_income = income - tax_revenue = 0.0 Step 2: Assemble demand with the public sector: aggregate_demand = autonomous_expenditure + government_spending + marginal_propensity_to_consume * disposable_income = 5.0 Final result: 5.0

worked_examples.question: Using Adding the Government: Taxes and Spending in Aggregate Demand, compute the result for income = 4, tax_revenue = 4, autonomous_expenditure = 4, government_spending = 3, marginal_propensity_to_consume = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Remove taxes from income: disposable_income = income - tax_revenue = 0.0 Step 2: Assemble demand with the public sector: aggregate_demand = autonomous_expenditure + government_spending + marginal_propensity_to_consume * disposable_income = 7.0 Final result: 7.0

concepts.title: Equilibrium Income: Ex Ante Demand Equals Output
concepts.definition: Income settles where planned output equals planned aggregate demand; solving that equality gives equilibrium income as autonomous spending divided by one minus the marginal propensity to consume, equivalently by the marginal propensity to save.
concepts.key_idea: At equilibrium, unplanned inventory change is zero, and income is a multiple of autonomous spending.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.3.2 algebraic method, equation 4.4, page 61
question_patterns: solve for equilibrium income given autonomous spending and the marginal propensity to consume
find the income level at which planned output matches planned demand
why is income in equilibrium a multiple of autonomous expenditure
an economy has autonomous spending 100 and MPC 0.75, what income results
show the algebra that turns Y equals A plus cY into the equilibrium formula
what stock behaviour signals that income is not at its equilibrium level

solution_steps.action: Convert the spending fraction to the saving fraction
solution_steps.explain: The denominator of the equilibrium formula is the share of extra income not spent.

solution_steps.action: Divide autonomous spending by the leak
solution_steps.explain: Setting Y equal to A plus cY and solving gives income as A over the saving fraction.

worked_examples.question: Using Equilibrium Income: Ex Ante Demand Equals Output, compute the result for marginal_propensity_to_consume = 3, autonomous_expenditure = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Convert the spending fraction to the saving fraction: marginal_propensity_to_save = 1 - marginal_propensity_to_consume = -2.0 Step 2: Divide autonomous spending by the leak: equilibrium_income = autonomous_expenditure / marginal_propensity_to_save = -1.5 Final result: -1.5

worked_examples.question: Using Equilibrium Income: Ex Ante Demand Equals Output, compute the result for marginal_propensity_to_consume = 4, autonomous_expenditure = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Convert the spending fraction to the saving fraction: marginal_propensity_to_save = 1 - marginal_propensity_to_consume = -3.0 Step 2: Divide autonomous spending by the leak: equilibrium_income = autonomous_expenditure / marginal_propensity_to_save = -1.333333 Final result: -1.333333

concepts.title: Investment Multiplier and the Round-by-Round Mechanism
concepts.definition: An extra rupee of autonomous spending becomes someone's income, part of which is re-spent, feeding further rounds; the total income rise is a multiple - one over the saving fraction - of the initial outlay, so a 10-unit rise with MPC 0.8 lifts income by 50.
concepts.key_idea: Each round re-spends the MPC fraction of the last, and the geometric series sums to the multiplier times the first shock.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.3.3, Table 4.1 and equation 4.5, pages 62-63
question_patterns: calculate the change in equilibrium income from an increase in autonomous investment
find the value of the investment multiplier for a given MPC
explain how one firm's extra spending becomes many rounds of income
investment rises by 20 with MPC 0.8, by how much does income rise
why does a higher marginal propensity to consume enlarge the multiplier
sum the infinite rounds of spending to get the total income change

solution_steps.explain: The multiplier is one divided by the fraction of each round's income that leaks into savings.
Multiplying the multiplier by the change in autonomous investment gives the total change in equilibrium income.

worked_examples.question: Using Investment Multiplier and the Round-by-Round Mechanism, compute the result for marginal_propensity_to_save = 3, change_in_autonomous_investment = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Invert the saving leak: investment_multiplier = 1 / marginal_propensity_to_save = 0.333333 Step 2: Scale the initial shock: change_in_income = investment_multiplier * change_in_autonomous_investment = 1.0 Final result: 1.0

worked_examples.question: Using Investment Multiplier and the Round-by-Round Mechanism, compute the result for marginal_propensity_to_save = 4, change_in_autonomous_investment = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Invert the saving leak: investment_multiplier = 1 / marginal_propensity_to_save = 0.25 Step 2: Scale the initial shock: change_in_income = investment_multiplier * change_in_autonomous_investment = 1.0 Final result: 1.0

concepts.title: Paradox of Thrift
concepts.definition: When everyone tries to save a larger slice of income, aggregate demand falls, output contracts through the multiplier, and the economy can end up with aggregate savings no higher - or lower - than before, because one person's saving is another person's lost income.
concepts.formula: aggregate_savings = investment (unchanged in equilibrium despite higher thrift)
concepts.key_idea: Virtue for one household, vice for the economy: universal thrift shrinks income without raising total savings.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.3.3, paradox of thrift example, pages 63-64
question_patterns: explain the paradox of thrift with the help of the Keynesian model
what happens to total savings when every household decides to save more
why can an economy end up saving the same after a rise in thrift
trace the rounds through which higher saving lowers income
when MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.5 what happens to equilibrium output
contrast the effect of thrift on one household and on the whole economy

solution_steps.explain: A rise in the saving propensity cuts consumption demand at the existing income level, creating excess supply.
Producers cut output, factor incomes fall, and spending shrinks again by the new MPC fraction each round.
At the new lower equilibrium, aggregate saving equals investment just as before, so total savings are unchanged or smaller - the paradox.

concepts.title: Full Employment, Deficient Demand and Excess Demand
concepts.definition: The income at which demand equals output need not be the income at which everyone has work: if equilibrium sits below the full-employment level, demand is deficient and prices tend to sag; if it sits above, demand is excessive and prices tend to climb.
concepts.key_idea: Equilibrium only means no pressure to change; it does not guarantee full employment.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.4, full employment paragraphs, page 65
question_patterns: does equilibrium income always mean full employment income
what is deficient demand and what does it do to prices
define excess demand and its long-run price effect
compare equilibrium output with full employment output
why can an economy rest in equilibrium with unemployed workers
name the situation where demand falls short of full employment output

solution_steps.explain: Find the demand-determined equilibrium output and the output possible when all factors are employed.
Equilibrium below full employment is deficient demand; above it is excess demand.
Deficient demand pulls prices down in the long run while excess demand pushes them up.

concepts.title: Effective Demand Principle and Parametric Shifts
concepts.definition: With prices and the interest rate fixed and supply perfectly elastic, output is dictated entirely by aggregate demand - the effective demand principle; on the diagram, a change in autonomous spending slides the AD line in parallel while a change in the propensity to consume swings it by altering its slope.
concepts.key_idea: Demand rules supply in the short run, and parameters move the AD line differently - parallel shifts versus swings.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec104.txt, section 4.4 summary paragraph and section 4.3.2 shift discussion, pages 61-65
question_patterns: state the effective demand principle and the assumptions behind it
how does the AD line move when autonomous spending rises
what happens to the demand line when the marginal propensity to consume falls
distinguish a parametric shift from a swing of a line
why does output respond only to demand in the fixed price model
explain what happens to equilibrium when the intercept increases versus when the slope decreases

solution_steps.action: Fix the price and interest backdrop
solution_steps.explain: With unused resources, extra output costs no more to make, so the price level can be held constant and supply is perfectly elastic.
Equilibrium output then equals planned aggregate demand, which is the effective demand principle.
A parameter change in A moves the line parallel up or down; a change in c rotates it, steepening or flattening the swing.

worked_examples.source_ref: leec104.txt section 4.3.2 example with C and I
worked_examples.question_pattern: An economy has consumption 60 plus 0.75 times income and investment fixed at 40. Find its equilibrium income.

solution_template.explain: One minus 0.75 leaves a saving fraction of 0.25.
100 divided by 0.25 gives equilibrium income of 400.

worked_examples.question_pattern: With MPC equal to 0.8, autonomous investment rises by 20. Find the multiplier and the total rise in income.

solution_template.explain: One over 0.2 gives a multiplier of 5.
5 times 20 gives a total income rise of 100.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Autonomous expenditure is 50 crores, MPS is 0.2 and income is 4000 crores. Measure the ex ante aggregate demand and say whether the economy is in equilibrium.

solution_template.action: Ex ante demand at that income

solution_template.explain: Planned demand of 3250 falls short of output 4000, so the economy is not in equilibrium; unsold stocks pile up.
